segments.text: Petroleum geology applies rock, structural, and stratigraphic principles from earlier chapters specifically to understanding how hydrocarbons form, move, and accumulate in economically extractable quantities — one of the most directly applied and economically significant branches of geology.

blocks.text: 1. Petroleum system elements: source, reservoir, seal, and overburden

segments.text: A complete
petroleum system
requires four essential elements acting together, in the correct spatial and temporal relationship: a
source rock
(fine-grained, organic-rich sedimentary rock, typically shale, where hydrocarbons originally form), a
reservoir rock
(porous and permeable rock, point 3, capable of storing significant hydrocarbon volumes), a
seal (cap) rock
(impermeable rock, typically shale or evaporite, preventing hydrocarbons from escaping further upward), and sufficient
overburden

(overlying rock providing the burial depth, and therefore heat and pressure, needed for hydrocarbon generation, point 2). The absence or failure of any single one of these four elements typically means no economically viable accumulation forms, regardless of how favourable the other elements might be.

blocks.text: 2. Generation, migration, and accumulation of hydrocarbons

segments.text: Generation
occurs when a source rock is buried deeply enough to reach the necessary temperature range (the “oil window”) for its organic matter (kerogen) to thermally break down into hydrocarbons.
Migration
is the subsequent movement of these hydrocarbons —
primary migration
out of the tight source rock itself, and
secondary migration
through more permeable carrier beds — driven mainly by buoyancy, since hydrocarbons are less dense than the surrounding formation water.
Accumulation
occurs where migrating hydrocarbons encounter a
trap
(point 4) that halts further upward or lateral migration, allowing them to concentrate in a reservoir rock rather than continuing to migrate all the way to the surface and being lost.
Porosity
is the percentage of a rock’s total volume that consists of open pore space, determining how much fluid (oil, gas, or water) it can potentially store.
Permeability

is a separate property measuring how well those pore spaces are interconnected, determining how easily fluid can actually flow through the rock. Critically, high porosity does not guarantee high permeability (or vice versa) — a rock can have abundant but poorly connected pore space (high porosity, low permeability, storing fluid but yielding it only very slowly) or well-connected pores (allowing good fluid flow) despite comparatively modest total porosity — making both properties essential and independent considerations for reservoir quality assessment.
A
trap
is any subsurface geological configuration that halts hydrocarbon migration and allows accumulation.
Structural traps

arise from tectonic deformation (Chapter 4) — most commonly an anticline (hydrocarbons rise buoyantly to accumulate at the fold’s crest, beneath the seal), or a fault juxtaposing permeable reservoir rock against an impermeable seal rock.
Stratigraphic traps

arise instead from lateral or vertical changes in rock type or depositional geometry (rather than from later tectonic deformation) — such as a reservoir sandstone body that pinches out laterally into impermeable shale, or is truncated beneath an unconformity (Chapter 2) sealed by overlying impermeable rock.
Petroleum exploration proceeds through progressively narrowing, increasingly costly and precise stages:
regional basin analysis

(assessing a large sedimentary basin’s overall geological history and hydrocarbon potential, often guided by sequence stratigraphy, Chapter 7), followed by more detailed geophysical surveying (particularly seismic methods, Chapter 6, used specifically to image subsurface structures and potential traps), and finally exploratory drilling to directly confirm (or rule out) the presence of an actual hydrocarbon accumulation predicted by the earlier stages — each stage is specifically designed to reduce geological uncertainty before committing to the next, more expensive stage.

Pakistan’s petroleum geology involves specific sedimentary basins (such as the Indus Basin) with their own particular source rocks, reservoir intervals, and trap types, and its hydrocarbon exploration and production figures change over time as new discoveries are made and existing fields deplete — for current, accurate figures and basin-specific detail, referring to the latest publications of the Geological Survey of Pakistan, the Petroleum Division, or other authoritative official sources is essential, since such administrative and production details are genuinely subject to ongoing change.

items.text: A complete petroleum system requires source, reservoir, seal, and sufficient overburden together; the absence of any one element typically prevents accumulation.
Generation requires adequate burial/heat, migration is driven mainly by buoyancy, and accumulation requires an effective trap to halt further migration.
Porosity (storage capacity) and permeability (flow capacity) are distinct, independent properties, both essential to assessing reservoir quality.
Structural traps arise from tectonic deformation (folds, faults); stratigraphic traps arise from lateral/vertical rock-type changes or unconformities, without requiring later deformation.

Petroleum exploration proceeds through progressively more detailed and costly stages (basin analysis, geophysical surveying, drilling), each reducing uncertainty before the next; current Pakistani figures should be verified against official Geological Survey of Pakistan or Petroleum Division sources.
